scams.name: Scopolamine (Burundanga) Drugging
scams.city: Bars and clubs in El Poblado
scams.description: You're having a great night at a bar near Parque Lleras when an attractive local — often a woman — begins chatting with you and offers to buy you a drink. The drink has been spiked with scopolamine, a drug derived from a local plant that causes total compliance and memory loss. You wake up hours later having handed over all your cash, PIN numbers, and valuables while fully conscious but unable to resist.
scams.avoidance: Never accept drinks from strangers you just met in Medellín nightlife | Order your own drinks at the bar and watch them poured | Go out in groups and look out for each other — scopolamine victims appear functional but aren't

scams.name: Express Kidnapping by Fake Taxi
scams.description: You hail a taxi on the street late at night and get in without thinking. The driver takes an unexpected route and suddenly you're locked in the car with additional men who take your phone and wallet. They drive you to ATMs and force withdrawals until your accounts are empty, then leave you somewhere unfamiliar. This 'paseo millonario' (millionaire's walk) is a documented Medellín crime pattern.
scams.avoidance: Use Uber or InDriver exclusively — never hail a street taxi in Medellín under any circumstances | Have the Uber app open before you need it so you're not tempted to wave down a car | Ask your hotel to call a trusted taxi company if apps aren't available

scams.name: Phone Snatching in Public
scams.description: You're walking through Laureles or El Centro with your phone in your hand looking at Google Maps when someone on a motorbike drives onto the sidewalk, snatches your phone without slowing down much, and is gone before you process what happened. Phone theft by motorbike is extremely common throughout Medellín and locals have had their phones stolen this way multiple times.
scams.avoidance: Keep your phone in your pocket, bag, or pocket when walking on streets | Use Google Maps offline so you don't need to look at your phone constantly | If you need to use your phone, step inside a café or shop to do so

scams.name: Fake Drug Deal & Police Setup
scams.description: A man approaches you offering drugs at a friendly price. Shortly after you interact with him, men claiming to be police officers arrive and threaten to arrest you. They offer to make the whole thing go away for a 'fine' paid directly to them in cash — often $200-500. Both the seller and the 'police' are working together.
scams.avoidance: Do not engage with anyone offering drugs on the street — walk away immediately | Real Colombian police wear uniforms — plain-clothes officers showing cash fines are almost always scammers | If detained by someone claiming to be police, ask loudly for their badge number and say you'll go to the station

scams.name: Tinder/App Robbery Setup
scams.city: Apartments and unfamiliar locations in the city
scams.description: You match with an attractive person on Tinder or similar apps who quickly suggests meeting at their apartment. You arrive, things seem to be going well, and then associates emerge and rob you at knifepoint — or you're given a scopolamine-spiked drink and wake up to find everything gone. This is one of the most reported crime methods against male tourists in Medellín.
scams.avoidance: Always meet Tinder matches in busy public places first | Verify the person is real through a video call before meeting | Never go to a private apartment for a first meeting with someone you met online in Medellín

scams.name: Overpriced Tour to Pablo Escobar Sites
scams.description: You want to visit the sites associated with Pablo Escobar — a major draw for many visitors. A tout near your hostel offers a tour for $80 per person. You later discover the same tour runs for $20-30 through established operators, and that some unofficial 'guides' have no actual knowledge and are simply charging premium prices for access to locations that are public anyway.
scams.avoidance: Book Pablo Escobar tours through registered agencies like Paisa Road or Real City Tours | Compare prices on GetYourGuide or Viator before booking anything locally | Be aware that some Escobar family members run 'authentic' tours — research the ethics before booking

cultural.tipping: 10% propina (tip) is customary at sit-down restaurants and often added to the bill as 'propina voluntaria' — check before adding more. Tip taxi drivers by rounding up the fare. Hotel porters $1-2 USD per bag.
cultural.dressCode: Colombians dress smartly — looking presentable is a sign of respect. Avoid overly casual dress in cities. Medellin has a reputation for fashion-consciousness. Warmer coastal regions are more casual.
cultural.greetings: One cheek kiss between women and between men and women. Men shake hands. 'Buenos días/tardes/noches' always. First-name basis after introduction. Personal space is closer than Northern Europe/North America.
taboos: Discussing drug trafficking or Pablo Escobar with locals — deeply sensitive and offensive
Assuming Colombia is dangerous everywhere — locals are proud of the country's transformation
Wearing expensive jewelry or displaying phones in crowded areas
Declining food or drink offered by a host — very rude
Calling people 'negro' or commenting on race — contextually complex, avoid
Drinking tap water outside Bogotá, Medellín, and main cities
cultural.haggling: Acceptable in markets and with street vendors. Not appropriate in established shops or restaurants.

safety.lgbtSafety: Legal and increasingly accepted in major cities (Bogotá, Medellín). Same-sex marriage legal. More conservative in rural areas.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Exercise increased caution. Solo female travel is common in tourist areas but requires awareness. Avoid traveling alone at night, especially in less-touristed areas.
safety.notes: Colombia has transformed enormously but petty crime (phone snatching, bag theft) remains high in cities. Use Uber or InDriver over street taxis. Avoid displaying valuables. Bogotá's La Candelaria and Medellín's city center require vigilance at night.

scams.name: The Express Kidnapping Taxi
scams.description: You hail an unofficial taxi outside the airport or your hotel and get in. Shortly after, a second person gets in the car — sometimes claiming to be another passenger. Suddenly you realize you're being driven somewhere you don't recognize, and the 'passengers' demand you hand over your phone, wallet, and your bank card PIN. They drive you to an ATM and force you to withdraw cash. These express kidnappings typically last 2-3 hours.
scams.avoidance: Book taxis through your hotel or use InDriver/Uber | Never get into an unmarked vehicle | If in a bad situation, stay calm — express kidnappings in Lima are usually 'safe' as long as you comply and don't resist

scams.name: The Fake Tour Operator
scams.description: You book a Machu Picchu or Sacred Valley tour through a budget agency on the main Miraflores strip. They show you glossy photos and promise everything is included — train, bus, entry ticket. Days later in Cusco, you discover the train ticket was for a different time, the entry to Machu Picchu wasn't actually included, or the tour simply doesn't exist. You're out hundreds of dollars with no recourse.
scams.avoidance: Book Machu Picchu only through the official site tuboleto.cultura.pe | Use well-reviewed operators on TripAdvisor or verified by your hotel | Get every inclusion in writing with a receipt

scams.name: The Predatory Pricing
scams.description: You stop to buy something at a market stall or eat at a small restaurant without checking the menu. The vendor names a price only after you've already committed, and it's 5-10x what locals pay. When you push back, they get hostile or cause a scene. This 'gringo pricing' is especially common in tourist markets but also happens at unlicensed restaurants near Larco Mar.
scams.avoidance: Always confirm prices before committing | Eat at restaurants with menus and listed prices | Learn basic price phrases in Spanish

scams.name: The Mustard Smear
scams.description: Someone 'accidentally' squirts something on your shirt — mustard, bird poop, or colored water. An immediately helpful stranger produces tissues and starts cleaning you off. Meanwhile, their partner has unzipped your bag or picked your pocket. By the time you realize what happened, your camera or wallet is gone.
scams.avoidance: If something hits you, step away from all strangers immediately and check your belongings first | Keep your bag in front of you in crowded areas | Decline all unsolicited 'help'

scams.name: The Fake Police ID Check
scams.description: Two men — one in plain clothes, one in what looks like a police uniform — stop you and say there's been a drug incident nearby and they need to verify your money isn't counterfeit. One takes your wallet to 'inspect the bills' and returns it, but not before swapping large bills for smaller denominations or memorizing your card numbers.
scams.avoidance: Real Peruvian police don't conduct 'money inspections' on the street | Offer to walk to the nearest police station instead — they will refuse | Ask to see a badge and official ID number (real officers won't object)

scams.name: The ATM Helper
scams.city: ATMs near tourist areas in Miraflores and Barranco
scams.description: You're struggling with a Spanish-language ATM and a friendly bystander offers to help. They press some buttons 'to help you navigate the menu' — but while they're guiding you through, they're actually watching your PIN. Sometimes there's an actual device on the machine, other times they rely purely on observation. A few hours later your account is cleaned out.
scams.avoidance: Always shield your PIN with your body and hand | If someone approaches at an ATM, cancel your transaction and find another machine | Use ATMs inside bank branches only

cultural.dressCode: Casual in Lima and tourist towns. Layers essential for Andean altitudes (cold mornings and nights even in summer). Respectful dress at Andean communities and ruins. Comfortable, breathable clothing for jungle (Iquitos, Manu).

Taking photographs at Andean communities without permission

healthcare.summary: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Brazil. Emergency numbers (192/190/193), pharmacy tips, yellow fever vaccination, restricted medications, and travel insurance advice.
healthcare.costForTourists: Brazil's public healthcare system (SUS) provides free treatment to everyone including tourists, but is often overwhelmed with long waits. Private hospitals in major cities charge $80-200 USD for consultations and offer much higher quality.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Comprehensive travel insurance is essential. Private healthcare is significantly better than public, and emergency evacuation coverage is recommended for travelers visiting remote areas like the Amazon.
healthcare.vaccinationsRecommended: Yellow fever vaccination is strongly recommended and may be required for entry from certain countries; it's essential if visiting the Amazon, Pantanal, or rural areas. Hepatitis A, typhoid, and routine vaccinations should be current.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro have world-class private hospitals like Hospital Albert Einstein and Copa D'Or. In rural and Amazonian areas, medical facilities are very limited and evacuation may be necessary for serious conditions.

medications.prescriptionRules: A Brazilian prescription is required for prescription medications. Foreign prescriptions are not accepted. Antibiotics and many other drugs are widely available OTC. Carry medications in original packaging with a doctor's note.

safety.lgbtSafetyNote: Brazil has legal protections and a vibrant LGBT scene in major cities, but homophobic violence remains a serious concern, particularly outside São Paulo and Rio's tourist zones.

safety.violentCrime: Violent crime including armed robbery, carjacking, and mugging is a significant concern, particularly in favelas, urban peripheries, and at night. Brazil has one of the highest homicide rates in the world, though most violence is gang-related and concentrated in specific areas.
safety.soloFemaleSafetyNote: Solo female travelers should exercise heightened caution, especially at night and on beaches. Sexual harassment and assault do occur; stick to well-lit populated areas and use ride-hailing apps.
safety.notes: Brazil requires heightened awareness of personal security. Avoid displaying valuables, use hotel safes, and don't resist if robbed. risks.name: UV radiation

risks.name: Hantavirus

risks.name: Waterborne illness

healthcare.costForTourists: Chile has both public (FONASA) and private (ISAPRE) healthcare systems. Tourists should use private clinics where a consultation costs $60-120 USD; emergency public care is available but may involve waits.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Travel insurance with medical coverage is strongly recommended. Evacuation coverage is important for travelers heading to Patagonia or the Atacama Desert, where medical facilities are distant.
healthcare.vaccinationsRecommended: No special vaccinations are required for Chile. Routine vaccinations should be up to date, and hepatitis A is recommended for most travelers.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Santiago has excellent private hospitals including Clínica Alemana and Clínica Las Condes with modern facilities and English-speaking doctors. Outside Santiago, healthcare quality is adequate but more limited in remote areas like Patagonia.

medications.generalAdvice: Chile follows INCB international conventions. Carry certified prescriptions for controlled substances — ideally apostilled or with official translation. Keep all meds in original packaging.

safety.pettyCrime: Pickpocketing and bag theft are common in Santiago, Valparaíso, and tourist areas. Car break-ins and theft from parked vehicles are frequent, especially near trailheads and scenic viewpoints.

safety.soloFemaleSafetyNote: Chile is generally considered one of the safer Latin American countries for solo female travelers, with well-established tourism infrastructure and relatively low rates of gender-based violence against tourists.
safety.notes: Chile is one of the safest countries in South America for tourists. Be vigilant about petty theft in urban areas, especially around markets and public transport. travelAdvisory.summary: Exercise normal precautions in Uruguay. Uruguay is the safest country in South America with low crime rates by regional standards. Petty crime exists in Montevideo and beach resort areas. The main concern is petty theft.

travelAdvisoryUK.summary: Uruguay is generally safe. Take normal precautions against petty crime in cities. Protests may occur near government buildings. Beach areas can be crowded in summer — watch for jellyfish and rip currents.

healthcare.systemType: Mixed public (ASSE) and private mutual insurance (mutualistas) system. Private clinics recommended for tourists.
healthcare.costForTourists: Private clinic visit $50-120. Hospital admission $200-600/night. Medical care is much more affordable than Argentina or Brazil. Good quality private clinics available.
healthcare.pharmacyAccess: Pharmacies (farmacias) widely available and well-stocked. Emergency pharmacies rotate 24-hour coverage. Pharmacists speak Spanish — limited English.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Hospital Británico and Hospital Italiano in Montevideo are the best facilities for tourists. Public hospitals (Hospital de Clínicas) are overstretched — use private clinics for non-emergency care.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Travel insurance recommended. Uruguay has good healthcare by South American standards but private clinics require payment upfront. Insurance ensures access to best facilities.

controlledSubstances.note: Uruguay was the first country to fully legalize recreational cannabis (2013). Licensed pharmacies sell cannabis to residents. Tourists cannot legally purchase from pharmacies but enforcement is relaxed.
Carry original prescription and doctor's letter. Subject to customs inspection for quantities beyond personal use.
Available with prescription. Carry documentation for customs purposes.

medications.generalAdvice: Uruguay has progressive drug laws. Cannabis is legal but officially restricted to residents. Bring adequate prescription medication supplies. Most common medications available in pharmacies.

scams.name: Currency exchange at airport
scams.description: Airport exchange counters offer poor rates compared to city exchange houses (casas de cambio) or ATMs. The difference can be 10-20%.
scams.avoidance: Exchange only a small amount at the airport for immediate needs. Use city exchange houses (casas de cambio) or Redbanc ATMs for better rates.

scams.name: Taxi overcharging for tourists
scams.description: Some taxi drivers take circuitous routes or use tampered meters for foreign tourists, particularly from Carrasco Airport.
scams.avoidance: Request that the meter is used (taxímetro) or use Uber (available in Montevideo). Agree on price before departure for longer trips.

scams.name: Diversion pickpocketing
scams.description: A person creates a distraction (spills something, asks for directions) while an accomplice picks pockets or grabs bags.
scams.avoidance: Be alert when anyone invades your personal space unexpectedly. Keep valuables in front pockets or locked zipper bags. Be especially alert in crowded markets.

scams.name: Beach property theft
scams.description: Thieves target unattended bags, phones, and clothing at beaches, particularly when swimmers are in the water.
scams.avoidance: Never leave valuables unattended at beaches. Use beach lockers where available or take turns supervising belongings.

connectivity.simOptions: Tourist SIMs from Antel, Claro, or Movistar at Carrasco Airport and mobile phone shops. $10-20 for 5-15GB packages. Antel has best national coverage. eSIM via Airalo.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Good free WiFi in hotels, cafes, and restaurants. Free WiFi in many public plazas across Montevideo. Reliable internet throughout the country.
connectivity.bestOption: Antel SIM for best nationwide coverage. Free WiFi widely available in cities.

cultural.tipping: Expected in restaurants: 10% is standard. Leave cash on the table. Bar service: round up or leave change. Hotel porters: $1-2/bag. Taxis: round up or add 10%.
cultural.dressCode: Casual dress widely acceptable. Uruguay is relaxed and informal. Beachwear only at beaches. Smart casual for upscale restaurants.
cultural.greetings: Cheek kiss (one cheek) standard greeting between friends and when meeting women. Handshake for formal business introductions. 'Hola' and 'Cómo estás?' are common informal greetings. Uruguayans are warm and friendly.
taboos: Uruguayans are sensitive about comparisons with Argentina — do not suggest they are the same culture
Football (soccer) is a serious passion — tread carefully discussing opposing teams
Avoid political discussions about recent history
cultural.haggling: Not typical in Uruguay. Fixed prices observed in shops and restaurants. Some negotiation possible in antique markets or informal settings.

safety.lgbtSafety: Uruguay is the most LGBTQ+-friendly country in South America and one of the most progressive in the world. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013. Gender identity laws are progressive. Montevideo and Punta del Este are very welcoming.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Generally safe by South American standards. Uruguay has the lowest crime rate in the region. Take normal precautions in cities — avoid walking alone at night in less-touristed areas.
safety.notes: Uruguay is consistently ranked the safest country in South America. Crime rates are much lower than neighbors Argentina and Brazil. The main risks are petty theft in tourist areas and beach theft. Montevideo's Ciudad Vieja requires more caution after dark.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia, and most of the Americas receive visa-free entry for 90 days.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: December-March (austral summer, beach season at Punta del Este). May-September is mild and less crowded. Annual Carnaval in February is the longest in the world.
